first_impression.reaction: Googled 'wedding table settings' because the venue asked us to pick a setting and I wanted to know what's normal. The intro is a bit flowery ('tells them how the evening will run') but the second paragraph says what the page does, and the key takeaways are actual rules, not fluff. Jumped to the FAQ first: short, direct answers. Then it names its source, Emily Post, and admits it's an American reference, not Australian rules. That's more honesty than I expected from a styling article. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Before the florals arrive and the candles are lit, every guest sits down to the same small arrangement of plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and name card, and that arrangement tells them how the evening will run.
journey.reaction: Bit of mood-setting to open. Harmless, and the next paragraph gets to the point.

journey.quote: Either is correct: to the left of the forks or in the centre of the charger.
journey.reaction: Straight answer, no padding. FAQ is where I start and this one respects my time.

journey.section: The place setting, piece by piece
journey.quote: Treat them as a well-tested framework rather than a set of Australian rules, and adapt them to your menu.
journey.reaction: Named source, and they tell me its limits. That's exactly what I want to see. I can check Emily Post myself.

journey.quote: The most useful rule for a wedding is the simplest: only set the cutlery your guests will use.
journey.reaction: Practical, and it implicitly means 'don't let anyone sell you extra'. Good.

journey.section: Glassware, in the order it is used
journey.quote: If your drinks list runs to several wines, count the glasses before you choose a low, wide centrepiece, because both need the same strip of table.
journey.reaction: A real trade-off nobody mentions. This is the kind of thing that catches you on the day.

journey.quote: A metallic or cut-glass charger under fine white china with a narrow gold or platinum rim.
journey.reaction: Seven themes of nice-sounding pieces, not a single word on what any of it costs to hire or which looks push the bill up. For me this is the part where the page turns into a mood board.

journey.quote: If you have a venue in mind and want to know which of these looks it can carry, talk it through with our Wedded Concierge team.
journey.reaction: Sales prompt dropped in after a styling list. Not offensive, but it comes before the bit that actually helps me (the venue questions).

journey.section: Table settings for a destination wedding
journey.quote: Ask these questions early, and ask for the answers in writing.
journey.reaction: Yes. Got burned before on verbal promises. This is the most useful line on the page for me.

journey.section: Table settings for a destination wedding
journey.quote: Which pieces would need to be hired in for our theme and guest count?
journey.reaction: Good question, but the obvious follow-up is missing: what does each hired piece cost, and who supplies it? That's where the surprise line items live.

journey.section: Table settings for a destination wedding
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit, so the setting you approve is the setting your guests sit down to.
journey.reaction: Written confirmation is right. But 'the setting you approve is the setting your guests sit down to' is a promise with nothing behind it. And if you're arranging the hire-in, do you take a cut on it?

journey.section: What to check at the trial table
journey.quote: A mock-up is one table laid exactly as it will be on the day, and it is the hour that settles the reception.
journey.reaction: 'The hour that settles the reception' is a bit grand. The checklist underneath is solid though, especially sightlines and spacing.

journey.quote: Choose from what the venue holds first, then hire in what is missing.
journey.reaction: Sensible and cost-aware, even without saying so. Use what's included before paying for more. I'd have liked them to say that part out loud.

journey.section: Set the table with someone in your corner
journey.quote: With one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact, the questions to the venue, the mock-up and the final setting sit with one person who knows your plans.
journey.reaction: Fine as a description of the service, but 'someone in your corner' is a feeling. What does that person cost me, and what's in it for them?

unanswered_questions: Roughly what does hiring in chargers, glassware or themed cutlery add per guest, or at least which themes are typically the expensive ones?
When pieces are hired in for a destination wedding, who sources and supplies them? (deferred business detail)
Do you take a commission or mark-up on hire items or venue add-ons you arrange? (deferred business detail)
How is the Wedded Concierge fee calculated, and what does it cover for something like table styling? (deferred business detail)
Show me a real reception you've planned, with what the venue supplied versus what was hired and what it cost. (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit, so the setting you approve is the setting your guests sit down to.
turn_offs_found.why: Second half is a guarantee-style promise with no evidence. The written confirmation part is enough on its own.

turn_offs_found.quote: A mock-up is one table laid exactly as it will be on the day, and it is the hour that settles the reception.
turn_offs_found.why: Dramatic phrasing where a plain statement of purpose would do.

turn_offs_found.quote: Set the table with someone in your corner
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional heading on the sales section. Tells me how to feel instead of what I get.

would_share_with: My fiancee: the venue questions list and the 'when to decide each piece' order
Our Reddit thread: the 'only set the cutlery your guests will use' rule and the glasses-versus-centrepiece warning

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like that handled for you, our Wedded Concierge team can take the venue questions from here.
cta_reaction.why: Useful, honest how-to, and it earns a bookmark. But I came here for etiquette, not a planner, and nothing on the page tells me how the fee works or whether you earn on the hire-in. I'd ask the venue these questions myself before paying someone to do it.

top_3_changes: Add the cost follow-up to the venue questions. Old: "Which pieces would need to be hired in for our theme and guest count?" New: "Which pieces would need to be hired in for our theme and guest count, and what would each add to the quote?"

Cut the unsupported promise and keep the useful part. Old: "Your Wedded Advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit, so the setting you approve is the setting your guests sit down to." New: "Your Wedded Advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit."

Tone down the mood lines. Old: "and it is the hour that settles the reception." New: "and it is where any problems with the setting show up before the day." Old heading: "Set the table with someone in your corner" New heading: "Plan your table settings with a Wedded Advisor"

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types and severities limited to schema enums
Stayed in character as Daniel (sceptic): FAQ first, checked sources, hunted for costs, fees and commissions, flagged promises and mood lines
No invented brand facts; fees, commissions, supplier sourcing and real weddings voiced only as deferred unanswered questions
Suggested edits are exact old/new strings, add no new facts or measurements, and stay within deferred fee/commission/sourcing limits
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored

open_questions.question: The page has no cost signal at all for themes or hire-in. Is a cost question in the venue checklist (edit 1) acceptable, given the brand defers sourcing and hire detail? It asks the venue, it doesn't state any figure.

assumptions: Daniel arrived via Google for 'wedding table settings' with a venue asking him to choose a setting; informational intent, so relevance 3 and enquiry 2.
Business details (fees, commissions, supplier and hire sourcing, real weddings) are deferred; voiced as unanswered questions only, not as edits.
Rendered link text and bold labels quoted without markdown syntax, as a reader would see them.
Fast-mode read: intro, takeaways, FAQ, place setting rules, destination and planning sections read closely; theme lists skimmed.
